newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Agencies suspend Mogadishu aid over kidnap.
newsitem.headline: Agencies suspend Mogadishu aid over kidnap.

text.p: Non-governmental aid agencies halted "non-vital" operations in the Somali capital Mogadishu on Thursday to press for the release of a kidnapped Somali aid worker.
Their action from midnight (2100 GMT on Wednesday) followed a decision by U.N. aid agencies in the war-ravaged and divided city to suspend operations if Hilal Aden was not freed.
"Most of (our operation) is closed except vital aid because we cannot afford to let people die," said Jean-Marc Jouineau of Action against Hunger (ACF), the largest aid agency in the Somali capital.
North Mogadishu faction leader Ali Mahdi Mohamed, who heads Somalia's biggest clan alliance, said he did not know where Aden was and complained the aid suspension would hit the vulnerable.
"It is true that Mr Hilal Aden was kidnapped in Mogadishu north, but he was immediately transferred to somewhere else and we are in search of him," Ali Mahdi said in a statement.
The aid suspension followed a recommendation from the Somali Aid Coordination Body (SACB), which groups aid agencies and donors, for a shutdown unless Aden was released.

The SACB said Aden, an employee with the Swedish Life and Peace Institute (LPI), had been held without proper medical treatment despite being badly wounded when kidnapped in north Mogadishu on September 19.

Action Against Hunger (ACF) said it was closing a supplementary feeding operation that catered for more than 10,000 Mogadishu children, but was keeping open an essential feeding service for 300 others.
Witnesses said Aden, brother of a prominent clan politician, was shot while being kidnapped from his home in north Mogadishu by three unidentified gunmen.

Kidnappings and extortion are common in Mogadishu, a city awash with weapons and high unemployment since the collapse of a central government in 1991 after the overthrow of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre.
In a separate development, Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi handed over to the Australian High Commissioner in Nairobi an Australian pilot who was jailed in Somalia last May, diplomats said.
The pilot, Justin Fraser, 25, had been held by the south Mogadishu-based faction led by Hussein Aideed. Aideed succeeded his father, warlord Mohamed Farah Aideed, who died in August.
International aid agencies pulled out all foreign staff from southern Mogadishu earlier this year but kept some foreign staff in northern Mogadishu.
But aid agencies have a vital role in the capital, where food is too expensive for many families and essential services have broken down.
